items.item: ich-Laut and ach-Laut are one sound that changes with the vowel before it
The full ich-Laut context: front vowels, umlauts, ei/eu/äu, l/n/r
-chen is always the ich-Laut
The ach-Laut is velar or uvular
The ich-Laut is not sch
Word-final -ig is said with the ich-Laut in the northern standard
Initial ch in loanwords varies by region (China, Chemie)
The consonant r is usually uvular
After a vowel, r becomes a vowel glide (as in non-rhotic English)
-er is an a-like vowel [ɐ], kept distinct from -e [ə]
Schwa occurs only unstressed and often disappears before n/l
Obstruents are voiceless at the end of a syllable and voiced again before a vowel
It applies to syllable ends, not just word ends
The spelling ignores devoicing (stem spelling)
English has no final devoicing, so English speakers have to learn it
Devoicing is a northern feature, and the south sounds different
Fortis/lenis is the technical analysis behind voiced/voiceless
Each vowel-initial word starts with a glottal catch
It also appears inside words: before vowel-initial stems, and in hiatus before a stressed vowel
No linking across words, so mein Auto is not mei-Nauto
It is not a phoneme, and it is weaker or absent in the south, in Austria, in Switzerland and in casual speech
The glottal stop as a gender pause
